sections.name: General Knowledge
sections.note: Part 1 (VALR, DM, QADI) shares a combined 170-minute limit; GK is a separate 10-minute section with no negative marking.

items.passage: Speed is treated as a virtue in almost every domain: faster delivery, faster decisions, faster replies. Yet some things get worse when hurried. A doctor who rushes a diagnosis, a judge who rushes a verdict, a writer who rushes a draft: each trades accuracy for pace, and the cost appears later, in a missed condition, an unjust outcome, a muddled argument. Slowness is not laziness. It is the deliberate allocation of time to the parts of a task where error is expensive and reflection pays. The difficulty is that slowness looks identical to delay from the outside, and organisations that reward visible busyness punish the quiet worker who thinks before acting. The remedy is to distinguish speed that serves the goal from speed that serves the appearance of effort. Replying instantly to every message feels productive but fragments attention; taking an hour to think before a major decision feels idle but prevents a costly mistake. A mature culture does not ask whether work is fast or slow in general. It asks which parts deserve haste and which deserve care, and it protects the second from the pressure of the first.
items.question: The author's central claim is that
options: some tasks get worse when hurried and deserve deliberate time
all work should be done slowly
items.explanation: The passage says some things get worse when hurried and slowness is deliberate allocation of time where error is expensive. It does not claim all work should be slow or speed always harmful.

items.question: Slowness is defined in the passage as
options: the deliberate allocation of time where reflection pays
items.explanation: The passage explicitly says slowness is not laziness but deliberate allocation of time to parts where error is expensive and reflection pays. The other options are not the definition.

items.question: Why is slowness hard to protect in organisations?
options: Because slow workers are always less skilled
Because it looks like delay and visible busyness is rewarded
Because slow work costs more money
items.explanation: The passage says slowness looks identical to delay from the outside and organisations rewarding visible busyness punish quiet thinking. Skill, dislike of thinking and cost are not the stated reasons.

items.question: A mature culture, according to the author, would
options: ask which parts deserve haste and which deserve care
items.explanation: The closing sentence says a mature culture asks which parts deserve haste and which deserve care. Instant replies, banning fast decisions and hours measurement are opposite to the view.

items.passage: Economists often describe markets as neutral mechanisms, matching supply with demand. The description is accurate as far as it goes, and incomplete in the way that matters most. Markets do not only allocate goods; they also teach people what to value. When everything has a price, people begin to treat price as the measure of worth, and activities once done for duty, love or pride start to be judged by their payoff. Paying blood donors can reduce donations, not because people dislike money, but because payment changes the meaning of the act from generosity to transaction. Fining parents for late pickups can increase lateness, because a fine converts a moral obligation into a purchasable service. None of this proves markets are bad. It proves they are not neutral. A society that uses prices everywhere should expect its citizens to think in prices everywhere, and should therefore choose carefully which domains to price and which to protect. The question is not whether to have markets, but where their logic belongs.
items.question: The author's main point is that markets
options: shape what people value and are not neutral
should be abolished in all domains
are neutral mechanisms with no wider effects
items.explanation: The passage argues markets teach people what to value and are not neutral. Neutrality is rejected, abolition is not proposed, and always reducing generosity overstates the claim.

items.question: The blood donor example is used to show that
options: money has no effect on behaviour
payment can change the meaning of an act
items.explanation: The passage says paying donors can reduce donations because payment changes the meaning from generosity to transaction. Dislike of money, always falling and no effect are not the point.

items.question: The late pickup fine example illustrates that
options: a fine can convert a moral obligation into a purchasable service
parents do not care about punctuality
items.explanation: The passage says the fine converts a moral obligation into a purchasable service, increasing lateness. Always working, not caring and never fining are not the illustration.

items.question: The author would most likely support
options: choosing carefully which domains to price and which to protect
treating price as the measure of all worth
pricing every activity to improve efficiency
items.explanation: The closing advice is to choose carefully which domains to price and which to protect. Pricing everything, removing all prices and treating price as worth are opposite to the view.

items.question: Which option best weakens 'Online classes are as effective as classroom classes'?
options: A study found online students scored lower on the same tests despite similar ability
Classroom classes also use digital tools
items.explanation: Lower scores on the same tests despite similar ability directly challenges equal effectiveness. Saving time, preference and classroom use of tools do not address effectiveness.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to FRUGAL.
items.explanation: Frugal means careful with money and avoiding waste, so thrifty is the synonym. Wasteful and extravagant are opposites, and generous concerns giving rather than saving.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to OBSCURE.
items.explanation: Obscure means not well known or hard to understand, so clear is the opposite. Hidden, unclear and vague are synonyms or near synonyms.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to ZEAL.
items.explanation: Zeal means great energy or enthusiasm for a cause, so enthusiasm is closest. Apathy and doubt are opposites, and calm describes a different quality.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to COURAGEOUS.
items.explanation: Courageous means brave, so timid is the opposite. Brave, bold and daring are synonyms.

items.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: He is one of the best players who have played for the club.
He is one of the best players who has played for the club.
He is one of the best players whom have played for the club.
He is one of the best player who have played for the club.
items.explanation: One of the best players takes a plural noun and the relative clause verb agrees with players, so have is correct. Has mismatches the plural, player should be plural, and whom is the wrong case for a subject.

items.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: I have been working here since five years.
I have been working here since five year.
I have been working here from five years.
I have been working here for five years.
items.explanation: For is used with a duration such as five years, while since is used with a point in time. From is not used with the present perfect continuous in this way, and year should be plural.

items.question: Arrange the sentences in logical order. (1) The seed was planted in spring. (2) By autumn, the tree bore its first fruit. (3) The sapling was watered daily through summer. (4) The farmer pruned weak branches in July.
items.explanation: Chronology gives planting in spring, watering through summer, pruning in July, and fruit in autumn. Placing pruning before watering or fruit before growth breaks the seasonal sequence.

items.question: Which is the best summary of 'The firm cut costs by automating routine checks, but kept human review for complex cases, and errors fell while speed rose'?
options: Selective automation plus human review improved both speed and accuracy
items.explanation: The passage describes automating routine checks while keeping human review for complex cases, with errors falling and speed rising. The other options contradict the stated mix and outcomes.

items.question: A passage claims that reading fiction improves empathy because readers practise seeing the world through other minds. Which finding would most weaken this?
options: Empathy can also be learned at work
Fiction readers scored no higher on empathy tests than matched non-readers
items.explanation: Equal empathy scores between matched fiction readers and non-readers directly challenges the claimed effect. Enjoyment, workplace learning and sales do not test the causal claim.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to LUCID.
items.explanation: Lucid means easy to understand and clearly expressed, so clear and easy to understand is the synonym. Confusing, dark and complicated are opposites or unrelated.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to GENEROUS.
items.explanation: Generous means willing to give, so stingy is the opposite. Kind, liberal and charitable are synonyms or near synonyms.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The committee's decision was ______; no member raised an objection.
items.explanation: No member raising an objection means the decision was unanimous. Contentious, divisive and disputed all imply disagreement.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is necessary, with one c and double s. The other forms add or drop letters incorrectly.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is embarrass, with double r and double s. The other forms miss a doubled letter or add a wrong ending.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to PERSPICACIOUS.
items.explanation: Perspicacious means having keen insight and being able to notice and understand things that are not obvious. Keenly observant captures this meaning. Easily fooled is close to the opposite, while highly emotional and extremely wealthy describe unrelated qualities.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBDURATE.
items.explanation: Obdurate means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action, even in the face of persuasion. Stubborn is the closest synonym. Flexible is its antonym, generous describes giving rather than stubbornness, and cautious describes care rather than refusal.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to VITUPERATIVE.
items.explanation: Vituperative means bitter and abusive in language, full of blame and insult. Abusive is the closest synonym. Praising is the opposite, silent describes saying nothing, and cautious describes care, not hostility.

items.passage: A team regularly works late to meet deadlines. The manager praises long hours, and junior members feel they cannot leave on time without looking uncommitted. Productivity per hour is falling, and errors are rising. The manager must choose between celebrating hours, capping hours, or redesigning the workload.
items.question: What is the most likely cause of falling productivity per hour?
options: Sustained overwork causing fatigue and errors
items.explanation: Sustained overwork causes fatigue, which lowers output per hour and raises errors, matching the pattern described. Laziness, meeting count and leave do not explain the combined fall and error rise.

items.question: What should the manager do?
options: Ban all overtime immediately without changing deadlines
Cap routine late working, redesign the workload and deadlines, and judge performance by output not hours
items.explanation: Capping routine late work plus redesigning workload and judging by output addresses the cause while keeping delivery possible. More praise, a ban without deadline change and ignoring errors all preserve or worsen the overload.

items.question: Judging performance by hours rather than output is flawed because it
options: rewards presence over results and encourages performative overwork
items.explanation: Hours reward presence rather than results, so staff stay late to signal commitment even as output falls. Ease of measurement does not make it a good measure, and it does not motivate or reduce errors.

items.passage: A university researcher is offered funding by a firm whose product the research would evaluate. The funding would let the study proceed, but the firm wants the right to review results before publication. The researcher needs the funding and the publication for career progress.
items.question: What should the researcher do?
options: Accept the funding with pre-publication review by the funder
Accept funding only with a written agreement guaranteeing independent analysis and publication regardless of results
Publish only results the funder likes
items.explanation: A written agreement guaranteeing independent analysis and publication regardless of results protects the study's integrity while allowing funding. Funder review, blanket refusal and selective publication all compromise or abandon the research.

items.question: Pre-publication review by the funder is a problem because it
options: lets a party with a financial interest suppress unfavourable findings
items.explanation: A financially interested funder with review rights can delay or suppress unfavourable findings, which undermines trust in the results. Slowness, writing quality and universality are not the core problem.

items.question: What disclosure should accompany any published study?
options: Disclosure only if results are positive
Full disclosure of the funding source, the agreement terms, and any funder role in design or analysis
items.explanation: Full disclosure of funding, agreement terms and funder role lets readers judge bias for themselves. No disclosure, positive-only disclosure and salary disclosure all miss the relevant information.

items.passage: Two rival firms sell a similar product. One cuts its price below cost to drive the other out of the market. The smaller rival can match the cut and bleed cash, hold its price and lose customers, or differentiate on service and quality while accepting lower volume.
items.question: Which response best protects the smaller rival's survival?
options: Differentiate on service and quality, focus on loyal segments, and preserve cash
Copy the below-cost pricing and hope the rival fails first
items.explanation: Differentiation with a focus on loyal segments preserves cash and gives customers a reason beyond price to stay. Matching below-cost pricing bleeds cash, closing abandons the business, and hoping the rival fails first is a gamble on survival.

items.question: Below-cost pricing to drive out a rival is risky for the larger firm because it
options: burns cash, may attract regulatory scrutiny, and may fail if the rival survives on differentiation
items.explanation: Below-cost pricing burns the predator's cash, can draw regulatory attention, and fails if the rival survives by differentiating. It does not always succeed, raise profits at once, or lack downsides.

items.question: What should the smaller rival monitor most closely?
options: Cash runway, customer retention in its loyal segments, and the cost to serve them
items.explanation: Cash runway, retention in loyal segments and cost to serve determine whether differentiation can sustain the firm through the price war. Slogans, office size and likes do not measure survival.

items.passage: A university's largest donor asks the admissions office to admit his nephew, whose scores fall well below the cut-off. The donor hints that his next grant, which would fund fifty scholarships, depends on a favourable decision. The admissions head knows the university's rules allow no such exception, but the scholarships would transform many lives.
items.question: What should the admissions head do?
options: Admit the nephew quietly and keep the scholarships
Lower the cut-off for everyone so the nephew qualifies
Refuse the exception and explain that admission rules cannot be traded for donations
Ask the donor to wait a year and reapply
items.explanation: Admission rules exist precisely to stop wealth from buying places. A quiet admission betrays every rejected applicant, lowering the cut-off for everyone is a dishonest workaround, and delaying only postpones the same demand.

items.question: The argument that fifty scholarships justify one unfair admission is weak because
options: The nephew might fail his exams anyway
Scholarships are not popular with students
The donor's grant is smaller than the university budget
Trading one admission for funding turns a public trust into a private bargain and invites repetition
items.explanation: Once admission is traded for money, every future donor will expect the same, and the university's fairness is gone. Whether scholarships are popular, whether the nephew might fail, or how large the grant is does not change the principle.

items.question: How should the university handle the donor afterwards?
options: Thank him for past support, restate the admissions policy, and keep the scholarships conversation separate
Promise to reconsider the nephew next year
Cut off all contact with the donor immediately
Publicly name the donor as someone who tried to buy admission
items.explanation: The professional response is gratitude for past support, a clear restatement of policy, and a separate conversation about scholarships, which keeps the door open without conceding the principle. Cutting contact, public shaming and vague promises all handle the relationship worse.

items.passage: A customer returns a product after the 30-day return window, claiming it was faulty from the start. The store's policy is strict, but the customer has proof of purchase and a credible fault report from an independent technician. Refusing may lose a loyal customer and attract a public complaint; granting may encourage late returns.
items.question: What should the store do?
options: Accuse the customer of damaging the product
Refuse strictly by the policy with no exceptions
Grant returns to everyone without any time limit
Grant the return as a goodwill exception, record the fault evidence, and note the reason for the exception
items.explanation: A goodwill exception based on fault evidence, with a recorded reason, resolves a genuine case without abandoning the policy. Strict refusal ignores credible evidence, unlimited returns abandon the policy, and accusation without proof damages the relationship.

items.question: The late-return risk is best managed by
options: Recording the exception's specific grounds so future cases are judged against them, not against the exception itself
items.explanation: Recording specific grounds lets staff distinguish a fault-based exception from a general late return. Never granting, hiding and weekly changes all leave the policy unclear or inconsistently applied.

items.question: What matters most in the store's response?
options: The exact wording of the policy
The cost of the product alone
Whether the customer feels heard and the fault is addressed fairly
items.explanation: Feeling heard and a fair resolution of the fault determine whether the customer stays loyal, which is the real stake. Policy wording, following and product cost alone do not capture the service outcome.

items.passage: A listed firm's share price jumps after a rumour of a merger. The firm's communications head knows talks are at a very early stage and may fail. The head can confirm nothing, deny the rumour, or issue a holding statement that talks are preliminary and may not lead to a deal.
items.question: What should the communications head do?
options: Issue a factual holding statement that talks are preliminary, may not lead to a deal, and will be updated as required
Say nothing while insiders trade on the news
Deny the rumour outright to calm the market
items.explanation: A factual holding statement corrects the market's over-certainty without disclosing more than is appropriate, and commits to updates. Outright denial would be false, confirmation overstates early talks, and silence while insiders trade is unlawful and unfair.

items.question: Denying the rumour outright would be wrong because
options: denials always raise the share price
it would mislead investors who rely on the firm's statements
items.explanation: A false denial misleads investors who rely on official statements and creates legal exposure if the deal later proceeds. Denials do not always raise prices, rumours are not always true, and press preference is irrelevant.

items.question: What should the firm do about trading by its own staff during this period?
options: Enforce a trading blackout and remind staff of insider-trading rules
items.explanation: A trading blackout plus a reminder of insider-trading rules prevents staff from profiting on non-public information. Free trading, encouragement and ignoring all permit or invite insider trading.

items.passage: A firm uses an AI tool to screen job applications. The tool rejects far more applicants from one region than others. The vendor says the tool is proprietary and will not explain its criteria. HR likes the time saved; the hiring head worries about fairness and legal risk.
items.question: What should the firm do?
options: Delete all applications from the affected region
Keep using the tool because it saves time
Suspend the tool for screening decisions until its criteria and impact can be audited, using human review meanwhile
items.explanation: Suspending screening use until an audit is possible, with human review meanwhile, stops potentially unfair rejections while the firm investigates. Continuing, deleting applications and buying another opaque tool all preserve or worsen the problem.

items.question: The vendor's refusal to explain the criteria is a problem because
options: the firm cannot verify fairness or defend its decisions without understanding the criteria
items.explanation: Without understanding the criteria, the firm cannot verify fairness, correct errors, or defend decisions to rejected applicants or regulators. Free work, accuracy and HR preference are not the issue.

items.question: What should the firm require of any future hiring tool?
options: Explainable criteria, regular bias audits, and a human appeal route for rejected applicants
items.explanation: Explainable criteria, bias audits and a human appeal route make automated screening accountable. Lowest price, no human involvement and pure speed all sacrifice fairness for efficiency.

items.question: What is 12.5% of 640?
items.explanation: 12.5% is one-eighth, so 640/8 = 80. Recognising 12.5 percent as 1/8 makes the division immediate.

items.question: What is the least common multiple of 8 and 12?
items.explanation: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24 and of 12 are 12, 24, so the smallest common multiple is 24.

items.question: What is the value of 7^2 - 5^2?
items.explanation: 49 - 25 = 24. This is also a difference of squares, (7 - 5)(7 + 5) = 2 x 12 = 24, which agrees.

items.question: What is the average of the first 5 odd numbers?
items.explanation: The first five odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, whose sum is 25, so the average is 25/5 = 5.

items.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 4:7 and their difference is 18. What is the smaller number?
items.explanation: The difference of 3 ratio parts is 18, so one part is 6, and the smaller number is 4 x 6 = 24.

items.question: A and B together can do a job in 12 days. A alone can do it in 20 days. In how many days can B alone do it?
items.explanation: B does 1/12 - 1/20 = 1/30 of the job per day, so B alone takes 30 days. Subtracting A's rate from the combined rate leaves B's rate.

items.question: A train 200 metres long crosses a pole in 20 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
items.explanation: Speed is 200/20 = 10 m/s, which is 10 x 18/5 = 36 km/h. Converting m/s to km/h means multiplying by 18/5.

items.question: What is the simple interest on Rs 6000 for 4 years at 6% per annum?
items.explanation: Simple interest is 6000 x 6 x 4 / 100 = Rs 1440. Four years at 6 percent is 24 percent of the principal, and 24 percent of 6000 is 1440.

items.question: An article is sold for Rs 550 after a profit of 10%. What was its cost price?
items.explanation: The selling price is 110% of cost, so cost is 550/1.10 = Rs 500. Working backwards from a selling price means dividing by 1.10, not subtracting 10 percent of 550.

items.question: A boat in still water travels at 12 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. What is the upstream speed?
items.explanation: Upstream speed is still water speed minus stream speed, 12 - 3 = 9 km/h. The stream pushes against the boat when it travels upstream.

items.question: If x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0, what is the value of x?
items.explanation: The equation is (x - 3)^2 = 0, so x = 3, a repeated root. A perfect square trinomial has one root counted twice.

items.question: In an arithmetic progression the first term is 2 and the common difference is 5. What is the 8th term?
items.explanation: The nth term is a + (n - 1)d = 2 + 7 x 5 = 37. The 8th term adds seven common differences to the first term.

items.question: A card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is red?
items.explanation: There are 26 red cards in a deck of 52, so the probability is 26/52 = 1/2. Half the deck is red (hearts and diamonds) and half is black.

items.question: A rectangle has length 15 cm and breadth 8 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area is length x breadth = 15 x 8 = 120 sq cm. The area of a rectangle is the product of its two adjacent sides.

items.question: What is the remainder when 4^101 is divided by 3?
items.explanation: Modulo 3, 4 is 1, and 1 raised to any power is 1, so the remainder is 1. Any power of a number congruent to 1 modulo 3 is itself congruent to 1.

items.question: In how many ways can 3 students be chosen from a group of 8?
items.explanation: The number of combinations is 8C3 = 8 x 7 x 6 / 6 = 56. Order does not matter in a selection, so combinations divide the permutations by 3! = 6.

items.question: A right-angled triangle has legs 5 cm and 12 cm. What is the length of its hypotenuse?
items.explanation: By Pythagoras, the hypotenuse is sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13 cm. The 5-12-13 triangle is a standard Pythagorean triple.

items.question: If x + 1/x = 7, what is the value of x^3 + 1/x^3?
items.explanation: x^3 + 1/x^3 = (x + 1/x)^3 - 3(x + 1/x) = 343 - 21 = 322. The identity subtracts three times the original sum from the cube.

items.question: Two trains 180 m and 120 m long run towards each other at 72 km/h and 36 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other completely?
items.explanation: Relative speed is 72 + 36 = 108 km/h, which is 30 m/s. Total distance is 300 m, so the time is 300/30 = 10 seconds.

items.question: A vessel has 60 litres of mixture with milk and water in the ratio 3:2. How much milk must be added to make the ratio 4:1?
items.explanation: The mixture has 36 litres of milk and 24 litres of water. Adding x litres of milk gives (36 + x)/24 = 4/1, so 36 + x = 96, giving x = 60 litres.

items.question: What is the value of log10(1000) - log10(10)?
items.explanation: log10(1000) is 3 and log10(10) is 1, so the difference is 2. The difference of two logs is the log of the quotient, and 1000/10 = 100 = 10^2.

items.question: A cone has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. What is its slant height?
items.explanation: Slant height is sqrt(r^2 + h^2) = sqrt(49 + 576) = sqrt(625) = 25 cm. The radius, height and slant height form a 7-24-25 right triangle.

items.question: Which product had the highest total exports over the four quarters?

diagram.caption: Exports (Rs crore) of four products, Q1 to Q4

items.explanation: Adding the four quarters: X = 440, Y = 480, Z = 300, W = 430 crore. Product Y has the highest total at Rs 480 crore.

items.question: What is the percentage growth in Product X's exports from Q1 to Q4?
items.explanation: Product X's exports rose from Rs 80 crore in Q1 to Rs 140 crore in Q4, an increase of 60 crore. The percentage growth is 60/80 x 100 = 75%.

items.question: In which quarter were the combined exports of all four products the highest, and by how much did they exceed the lowest quarter?
items.explanation: The combined totals are Q1 = 360, Q2 = 370, Q3 = 440 and Q4 = 480 crore. The highest is Q4 at 480 and the lowest is Q1 at 360, so Q4 exceeds Q1 by 120 crore.

items.question: What is the overall percentage increase in total loans disbursed from 2023 to 2024?

diagram.caption: Loans disbursed (Rs crore) by four banks, 2023 and 2024

items.explanation: Total loans in 2023 were Rs 1800 crore and in 2024 they were Rs 1960 crore. The increase is 160 on a base of 1800, which is 8.9%.

items.question: Which bank recorded the highest percentage growth in loans disbursed?
items.explanation: Growth rates are: P 10.0%, Q 20.0%, R 10.0%, S -10.0%. Bank Q has the highest percentage growth at 20.0%.

items.question: What is the ratio of Bank R loans to Bank Q loans in 2024?
items.explanation: In 2024 Bank R disbursed Rs 660 crore and Bank Q disbursed Rs 480 crore, so the ratio is 660:480. Dividing both sides by 60 gives 11:8.

items.question: Which is the largest ocean in the world?
items.explanation: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean in the world, covering more area than all of Earth's land combined. The Atlantic is second, the Indian Ocean third, and the Arctic is the smallest.

items.question: What is the national flower of India?
items.explanation: The lotus is the national flower of India. The rose is a popular garden flower, jasmine is the national flower of Pakistan, and marigold is widely used in festivals.

items.question: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
items.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. A thermometer measures temperature, an altimeter measures altitude, and a hygrometer measures humidity.

items.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
items.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa. Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, Raphael painted the School of Athens, and Rembrandt painted The Night Watch.

items.question: Which is the smallest state in India by population?
items.explanation: Sikkim has the smallest population among Indian states. Goa is the smallest by area, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh have larger populations than Sikkim.

items.question: What is the boiling point of water at sea level?
items.explanation: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. The boiling point falls at higher altitudes where pressure is lower.

items.question: The headquarters of the International Labour Organization is located in which city?
items.explanation: The ILO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. Paris hosts UNESCO, Vienna hosts the IAEA, and New York hosts the UN headquarters.

items.question: Who wrote 'Midnight's Children'?
items.explanation: Salman Rushdie wrote 'Midnight's Children' and won the Booker Prize for it in 1981. V S Naipaul wrote 'A House for Mr Biswas', Amitav Ghosh wrote 'The Shadow Lines', and Vikram Seth wrote 'A Suitable Boy'.

items.question: Which is the largest producer of sugarcane in India?
items.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer of sugarcane in India. Maharashtra is second, Karnataka third, and Tamil Nadu is a smaller producer.

items.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the Uniform Civil Code?
items.explanation: Article 44, a Directive Principle of State Policy, directs the state to secure a uniform civil code for citizens. Article 42 is about just and humane conditions of work, Article 48 about animal husbandry, and Article 51 about international peace.

items.question: The Swadeshi Movement was launched in which year?
items.explanation: The Swadeshi Movement was launched in 1905 in response to the Partition of Bengal. The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920 and the Salt March in 1930.

items.question: Who discovered the structure of DNA?
items.explanation: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA in 1953. Mendel founded genetics, Pasteur worked on germs, and Fleming discovered penicillin.

items.question: Which is the largest producer of rubber in India?
items.explanation: Kerala is the largest producer of natural rubber in India. Tamil Nadu is second, Karnataka third, and Tripura is a smaller producer.

items.question: The headquarters of the New Development Bank (BRICS Bank) is located in which city?
items.explanation: The New Development Bank is headquartered in Shanghai, China. New Delhi hosts the AIIB office for India, Moscow is Russia's capital, and Beijing hosts the AIIB headquarters.

items.question: Who was the first Indian woman to win the Jnanpith Award?
items.explanation: Ashapurna Devi won the Jnanpith Award in 1976, the first woman to receive it. Mahadevi Varma won in 1982, Amrita Pritam in 1981, and Qurratulain Hyder in 1989.

items.question: Which gas is most abundant in the Earth's atmosphere?
items.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the Earth's atmosphere. Oxygen is about 21 percent, argon about 0.9 percent, and carbon dioxide about 0.04 percent.

items.question: The 'Cabinet Mission' came to India in which year?
items.explanation: The Cabinet Mission arrived in India in 1946 to discuss the transfer of power. The Cripps Mission came in 1942, independence came in 1947, and the Government of India Act was passed in 1935.

items.question: Which Indian state has the longest coastline?
items.explanation: Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian states, about 1,600 km. Andhra Pradesh is second, Tamil Nadu third, and Maharashtra is shorter.

items.question: Who wrote 'The Guide'?
items.explanation: R K Narayan wrote 'The Guide', which won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960. Mulk Raj Anand wrote 'Untouchable', Raja Rao wrote 'Kanthapura', and Khushwant Singh wrote 'Train to Pakistan'.

items.question: Which committee is associated with the recommendations on banking sector reforms in India?
items.explanation: The Narasimham Committee of 1991 and 1998 recommended banking sector reforms in India. The Kelkar Committee dealt with tax reforms, the Sarkaria Commission with Centre-state relations, and the Rangarajan Committee with disinvestment.

items.question: How many schedules did the Indian Constitution originally have?
items.explanation: The Indian Constitution originally had 8 schedules. It now has 12, after additions such as the Ninth Schedule in 1951 and the Tenth in 1985.

items.question: The 'Great Barrier Reef' is located off the coast of which country?
items.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Queensland, Australia, and is the world's largest coral reef system. Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand have coral reefs but not the Great Barrier Reef.

items.question: Who wrote 'Development as Freedom'?
items.explanation: Amartya Sen wrote 'Development as Freedom' in 1999. Jagdish Bhagwati wrote on trade, Pranab Bardhan on development economics, and Kaushik Basu on economics and game theory.

items.question: Which Indian won the first Dadasaheb Phalke Award?
items.explanation: Devika Rani received the first Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1969. Prithviraj Kapoor received it in 1971, Satyajit Ray in 1984, and Raj Kapoor in 1987.

items.question: The 'Roaring Forties' refer to what?
options: Strong westerly winds in the southern hemisphere
items.explanation: The Roaring Forties are strong westerly winds between 40 and 50 degrees south latitude, named by sailors for their strength. Ocean currents near the equator, monsoon winds and trade winds are different phenomena.
